notes.urn:cts:latinLit:stoa0128b.stoa009.opp-l: Several scanning errors corrected silently (e.g. 'æternæ vile' = aeternae vitae; 'coronat!' = coronati; 'renatus escreden-' = renatus es credens; 'esse. li s' = essentias; 'Commerabuntur' = commemorabuntur). Some printed scripture references are faulty: '1 John xi, 19' should be 1 John 2:19, 'Acts iv, 52' should be Acts 4:32. Psalm numbers follow the Vulgate as given. In chapter 3, 'in id quod aequalis est Patri' is construed as 'in that he is equal to the Father'; the phrase is somewhat awkward and may be corrupt.

Scanning errors read as evident: 'inuascibilis' as innascibilis, 'in uni- Me personæ' as in unitate personae, 'tu ibi ea' as tu ibi es, 'jacie' as facie. 'Spiritus Deus est' is cited by the edition as John 4:14; it is John 4:24. The quotation of 1 Corinthians 6:19 reads 'membra vestra' (your members), not 'corpus vestrum', and is translated as given. In 'Sed ne forte ... Deum esse abnegent' the singular 'he' refers loosely to either the Son or the Spirit.

Chapter VII: 'cloquio' read as 'eloquio', 'clementis' as 'elementis'. Chapter VIII: 'de Dei sui dono beatam, et per liberum arbitrium beatificatam non jugiter adhaerentem' is awkward; read as 'beatificatori' (clinging to the one who made it blessed), taken as not unceasingly clinging; the text may be corrupt. Chapter IX: 'expertus non esse' read as 'expertus non esset'. The Psalm cited as XIII, 6 is Psalm 29(30):6. Chapter XI: 'Non introducuntur nisi fideles, nisi baptizati fuerint' is elliptical; translated literally.

Ch. XII: the quotation 'Qui sibi nequam est, cui bonus' is Ecclesiasticus 14:5; the edition's reference 'IV, 5' appears to be a misprint. 'I, qui virtutem dedit' read as 'Ille, qui'. Ch. XIII: 'hos dicit ire in supplicium aeternum' refers to the wicked; the sentence seems compressed or partly corrupt. The final words 'in linc saeculo ... in regr' read as 'in hoc saeculo ... in regnum'; the text breaks off at the end.

nodes.text: THE BOOK OF ST FULGENTIUS TO FELIX THE NOTARY, ON THE TRINITY, IN ONE BOOK
CHAPTER ONE.

Since you, my dearest son Felix, kindled by the warmth of faith, ask me quite often how you ought to believe concerning the holy Trinity, which is God, or how you can defend the catholic and orthodox faith against the errors of the heretics, especially those whose company you keep, with the Lord's help, and so avoid their snares, I have thought it necessary and useful to you to answer your requests. But would that the unchangeable Trinity itself, in whose hand are both we and our words, might grant me, for proclaiming itself, right speech and sincere faith as fittingly and suitably as I wish, so that I may be able to satisfy in full your holy desire, burning with eagerness to learn. Believe, then, that we wish to make known to your most sincere mind that faith through which the patriarchs, the prophets, the apostles were justified and the martyrs crowned, which the holy Church holds to this day throughout the whole world, whose splendour, illuminating the minds of believers, makes them sharers in eternal life. This [faith] until now, through an unbroken line of succession, is preached in the chair of the apostle Peter at Rome and at Antioch, in the chair of Mark the evangelist at Alexandria, in the chair of John the evangelist at Ephesus, in the chair of James at Jerusalem, by the bishops of those cities. Compel, then, the Arians, Donatists, Nestorians, Eutychians, Manichaeans and the other plagues of heresy to enter into communion with these churches over which the apostles presided. They do not consent, because, divided from the unity of the Church by the depravity of their faith, they have chosen to be a faction. Hence the apostle John too says: They went out from us, but they were not of us. For if they had been of us, they would surely have remained with us (1 John 2:19). They went out from us indeed, because with a most unsound heart they separated themselves from the unity of the Church. They were not of us, that is, of the predestined, those chosen for eternal life. For they were not of those of whom the Lord says: I have chosen you and appointed you, that you should go and bear very much fruit, and that your fruit should remain (John 15:16). Nor are they blessed in the seed of Abraham, according to what the Lord said to Abraham: In your seed all nations shall be blessed (Genesis 26:4); and the Apostle, attaching [this], adds: Not to seeds, as of many, but to your seed, which is Christ (Galatians 3:16). Since all nations are found worthy to be blessed in Christ and through Christ into the unity of faith, the heretics are not blessed, because they do not have the unity of faith; but, fattened on the fodder of error, they have through pride become not sons of God but sons of the devil. Hence too, having the eyes of their heart darkened, they cannot see that the whole world has been redeemed by the blood of Christ and is of one accord in the unity of faith, according to what is described of the early Church: They had, it says, one heart and one soul towards God (Acts 4:32). So the whole world [is] redeemed; so the whole world, in all nations, is declared redeemed. And the nations shall fear your name, O Lord, it says, and all the kings of the earth your glory (Psalm 101:16). And again: All the nations whatever that you have made shall come and worship before you, O Lord (Psalm 85:9); or again: All the ends of the earth, it says, shall remember and turn to the Lord; and all the families of the nations shall worship in his sight. For the kingdom is the Lord's, and he shall rule over the nations (Psalm 21:28–29). What can the wretches say who, cut off from the Church of God, contradict that Church with an impenitent heart, and, while they strive to tear it, which is the seamless tunic of the Lord, are themselves more easily torn? Let them be questioned one by one. This one says he has been redeemed by the blood of Christ. So was the blood of Christ shed only for the Arians, or just for the Donatists? Far from it. Truth does not speak so. God does not speak so to Abraham: In your seed, he says, all nations shall be blessed (Genesis 26:4). Not one nation, but every one. Not this one and that, but all. Nor in differing faith, but in one, as the Apostle says: One faith (Ephesians 4:5). In one faith, that is, believers are saved; through the unity of faith the catholic Church has one heart and one soul towards God. This true faith, which makes the differing hearts of believers to be one, is praised by the mouth of the apostle Paul: I give thanks to God, he says, that your faith is proclaimed in the whole world (Romans 1:8). The one faith, which is proclaimed in the whole world, is the one to be praised and preached.
CHAPTER II

Receive the faith in which you were long ago reborn, believing in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. The Father is not the Son, the Son is not the Father, the Holy Spirit is neither the Father nor the Son. And since they are three, what, I ask, is the one name of the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit in which we must be baptised, if not that name of the Godhead, which cannot be tripled? For although we say God the Father, God the Son, God the Holy Spirit, yet we do not say three gods, because it is written: Hear, O Israel, the Lord your God is one (Deuteronomy 6:4). God, then, is one in nature, not in person, because the person of the Father is one, that of the Son another, that of the Holy Spirit another. The Father is begotten of no one, the Son is begotten of the Father, the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son. The Father is not [Father] to himself but to the Son; the Son is not [Son] to himself but to the Father; the Spirit is [the Spirit] of one who breathes: therefore he is referred to the Father and the Son. These relative names, then, make the Trinity; but the essential names are in no way tripled. God the Father, God the Son, God the Holy Spirit. Good the Father, good the Son, good the Holy Spirit. Merciful the Father, merciful the Son, merciful the Holy Spirit. Just the Father, just the Son, just also the Holy Spirit. Almighty the Father, almighty the Son, almighty also the Holy Spirit. And yet we do not say three Gods, nor three good, nor three merciful, nor three just, nor three almighty, but one God, good, merciful, just, almighty, the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit, in whom there is one nature, essence, or substance. For whichever of these names you speak of in that holy and supreme Trinity, it signifies one and the same thing. The essence of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit is not different. If it were, neither would the Son truly be begotten of the Father, nor would the Holy Spirit proceed from the Father and the Son. But because the Son is true, that is, begotten of the essence of the Father, the Holy Spirit too is true, proceeding from the Father and the Son. But if the Son or the Holy Spirit were of another kind than the Father, neither would the Son truly be the Father's, since a different essence would make him a stranger; likewise neither would the Holy Spirit proceed from the Father and the Son, which it is madness to say, because holy Scripture, in a faithful account, makes plain both that the Son is begotten of the Father and that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father.
CHAPTER III.

There are therefore three that are coeternal, consubstantial, coessential. But when the Fathers were asked, and it was said: Three what? they did not dare to say essences, or substances, or natures, lest some diversity of essences, or natures, or substances might perhaps be believed; but they said three persons, one essence, so that the one essence might declare the one God, and the three persons show the holy Trinity. Nor do we say this, that only the Trinity is God, and not each person. For the Father alone is God, and the Son alone is God, and the Holy Spirit alone is God. I say 'alone' because the Father is not the Son and the Son is not the Father, and the Holy Spirit is not the Father or the Son. But the inseparable, unchangeable, infinite Trinity does not admit three gods, just as it does not admit three essences, or substances, or natures; and therefore the Son, in that he is equal to the Father, is in no way to be called either created out of something or brought into being from nothing, because what the Father is, this he begot: God God, light light, the unchangeable the unchangeable, the infinite the infinite, the eternal the coeternal. Likewise concerning the Holy Spirit we believe that he is what that one is from whom he proceeds. Let us see, then, next whether we can prove what we have said by the testimonies of the holy Scriptures. First, too, it must be asked whether God is a Trinity. Let us make man, it says, in our image and likeness (Genesis 1:26). And again: Come, let us go down, it says, and confuse their languages there (Genesis 11:7). 'Our' and 'let us go down' indicate a plurality of persons, not of gods. Likewise the vision of Abraham, of three men, and his supplication to one Lord. And: The Lord rained upon Sodom and Gomorrah brimstone and fire from the Lord (Genesis 19:24). And: The Lord said to my Lord: Sit at my right hand (Psalm 109:1). And: By the Word of the Lord the heavens were established, and by the Spirit of his mouth all their power (Psalm 32:6). What else do these show but the Trinity? And more openly indeed the Lord in the Gospel: Go, baptise all nations in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit (Matthew 28:19). And again: A voice came from heaven saying: This is my beloved Son; hear him (Matthew 17:5). And likewise he says: I saw the Spirit of God descending like a dove and remaining upon him (John 1:32).
CHAPTER IV.

There you have in brief that the Father is one, the Son another, the Holy Spirit another; another and another in person, not another thing and another thing in nature; and for that reason, I and the Father, he says, are one (John 10:30). 'One' teaches us to refer to the nature, 'are' to the persons. Likewise this too: There are three, it says, who bear witness in heaven, the Father, the Word, and the Spirit, and these three are one (1 John 5:7). Let Sabellius hear 'are', let him hear 'three', and believe that there are three persons, and not blaspheme with sacrilegious heart by saying that he himself is his own Father, himself his own Son, himself his own Holy Spirit: as though in some way he begets himself, or in some way he himself proceeds from himself; when this cannot be found even in created natures at all, that something should be able to beget itself. Let Arius hear 'one', of course, and not say that the Son is of a different nature, since a different nature cannot be called 'one'. And so the Son cries out: I and the Father are one (John 10:30); and: He who sees me sees the Father also (John 14:9). And the Apostle [says] of him: Who, being in the form of God, he says, did not think it robbery to be equal with God (Philippians 2:6); and: For this reason, it says in the Gospel, the Jews sought to kill Jesus, because he not only broke the sabbath, but also called God his Father, making himself equal with God (John 5:18). And Arius contradicts with blasphemous spirit: They are not one, they are not equal, because the Son himself says of himself: The Father is greater than I (John 14:28); and he testifies again and again that he was sent by the Father. O unhappy error and pestilent doctrine, ignorant of the dispensation of the manhood, brought about in time for the salvation of the human race! I ask, in what respect is the Father greater than the Son? In substance, or in power, or in goodness, or in incorporeality, or in eternity? If God the Only-begotten is the image of God the unbegotten Father, the truth of a perfect and complete substance is in him, by which it comes about that he is the image of the truth. The Father is powerful, but if the Son is weak, he is no longer the image of one who is powerful. The Father is good, but if the Son is in a divinity of a different kind, the nature of something evil will not render the image of something good. The Father is incorporeal, but if the Son is bounded by a body in respect of spirit, then a corporeal being is not the form of one incorporeal. The Father is eternal, but if the Son is not coeternal, the name of fatherhood came to the Father in time; and then all things were not made through the Word, because a time is found earlier than the Word, when the Father was without the Son. But Scripture clearly declares the Word to be the image of God the Father, and all things to have been made through him. Or does he perhaps extend the sense of his impious profession so far as to believe that the Holy Spirit is good, but the Son better, and the Father best; or to assert with sacrilegious mind that the Holy Spirit is powerful, but the Son more powerful, and the Father most powerful; or to teach blasphemously that the Holy Spirit is just, but the Son more just, and the Father most just? Then he is not held within the profession of one God, but, after the manner of the heathen, is enslaved to the worship of many gods, while with rash presumption he supposes God the Father greater, and the Son lesser, and the Holy Spirit more than lesser. Let a greater God and a lesser God belong to the error of those who do not wish to be Israel, and with stopped ears do not hear: Hear, O Israel, the Lord your God is one God (Deuteronomy 6:4); and this: You shall worship the Lord your God, and him only shall you serve (ibid., 13).
CHAPTER V.

But lest perhaps with blinded heart they do not believe that the Son or the Holy Spirit is God, and, after the manner of the blaspheming Jews, deny that he is God, let them be refuted by the testimonies of the sacred Writings. Whose are the fathers, says the Apostle, and from whom is Christ according to the flesh, who is God blessed for ever (Romans 9:5). And again the apostle John: That we may be, he says, in his true Son Jesus Christ. He is the true God, and eternal life (1 John 5:20). And of the Holy Spirit John the evangelist [says]: The Spirit, he says, is God (John 4:14). And the Apostle, when he spoke of the Holy Spirit as the indweller of the Church: Do you not know, he says, that your members are the temple of the Holy Spirit? Glorify and bear the Lord in your body (1 Corinthians 6:19, 20). And in the Acts of the Apostles: Ananias, says Peter, why has Satan tempted your heart, that you should lie to the Holy Spirit (Acts 5:3)? And a little later he adds: You have not lied to men, but to God (ibid., 4). There he has the Son as God, the Holy Spirit as God. As for the Father, there is no need to prove that he is God, since he believes him to be God without doubt. But of the Son and of the Holy Spirit almost all holy Scripture resounds with this; but for brevity of discourse we have plucked a few [passages] from it. Now we believe the Son to be lesser, or sent, in the sense in which the Apostle also says: God sent his Son, made of a woman, made under the law (Galatians 4:4). 'Made of a woman', that is, born of the Virgin Mary: because he who was born of the Father without beginning received, by being born of a mother, a definite beginning in time. Who also, being in the form of God, says the Apostle, did not think it robbery to be equal with God, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, made in the likeness of men, and found in habit as a man, he humbled himself even to death, and the death of the cross (Philippians 2:6). 'Being in the form of God', he says, that is, being God in substance, he did not seize the Godhead, which he had by nature with the Father; but 'he emptied himself', that is, he did not appear to the human race in what he is as God and equal to the Father; but, with manhood assumed, not with God consumed, in the unity of his person he both appeared in this world and endured sufferings, and passed through without sin the human affections which were fitting and which he willed. According to this human form he is not equal to the Father, as he himself says: The Father is greater than I (John 14:28). But according to that by which he is equal to the Father, he says: I and the Father are one (John 10:30). According to the human form, he came into the world to save sinners (1 Timothy 1:15); according to the divine, he was in the world, and the world was made through him (John 1:10). And for that reason we must believe two substances, or natures, or forms (whichever of these you say, it is the same) in the one Son of God; one indeed of God, the other of man, so that the one Son of God may be believed to be true God and true man: lest, like Nestorius, introducing the man born of the Virgin Mary as a fourth person, we fall away from the Trinity; or, like Eutyches, not believing in a true man, we believe the Son of God to be without the assumption of manhood, that is, of one substance; or indeed suppose that from two substances one substance could have been made. For the Son of God, as we have said, assumed the whole man into the unity of his person, that is, a rational soul and flesh, according to what was said through the Prophet: Behold, a virgin shall conceive in the womb and bear a son, and his name shall be called (another reading: you shall call his name) Emmanuel (Isaiah 7:14), which is interpreted, God with us (Matthew 1:23). He therefore who was born of Mary is man and God; he who grew in age is man and God; he who was fixed to the cross is man and God, who also rose again, and ascended into the heavens, and sits at the right hand of the Father. And although, because of the unity of the person, God is man and man is God, yet it is according to the manhood that God is said to have been crucified, God is said to have suffered, God is said to have died. For according to what he is as God, he is rightly believed impassible and immortal.
CHAPTER VI.

Therefore each nature remains in Christ, preserving its truth, so that neither does the human, changed into the divine, cease to be man, nor is the divine changed into the human and cease to be God. Thus, then, one is begotten, the other created; one timeless, the other temporal; one without beginning, the other with a beginning. And although that begotten and timeless [nature] belongs to the Father and the Holy Spirit, the temporal and created by no means does: because in truth whatever of nature the Father has, he gave to the Son by begetting; whatever of nature came to the Son in time or from outside does not overflow to the Father or to the Holy Spirit. And though the whole Trinity is one substance, the man Christ does not belong to the whole Trinity, but only to the Son. For it is not lawful to believe that the Father or the Holy Spirit assumed manhood, or suffered according to manhood. Now the Holy Spirit, although he is nowhere found in the Scriptures to be lesser, is yet most evidently found written of as sent. On account of this the heretics bind their own necks, and, with the spirit of their understanding constricted, or rather suffocated, they do not acknowledge the Holy Spirit as their creator, while they define him to be a creature. If he were a creature, he certainly could not be a creator, because a creature does not form a creature from nothing. And since in Genesis God says that man was formed in his image (Genesis 1:27), and Job relates that he was fashioned by the Holy Spirit: The divine Spirit, he says, who made me (Job 33:4); it is clearly evident that the Holy Spirit is a fellow-worker with the Father and the Son, both in the forming of man and likewise in the establishing of the angels, according to that [saying] of the Psalmist: By the Word of the Lord the heavens were established, and by the Spirit of his mouth all their power (Psalm 32:6). If he is God, if he is creator, if he consecrates baptism, why is he said to be sent? He is called sent, of course, in that he came upon Christ in the form of a dove at the river, in that he came upon the apostles in fire. For the appearing itself is the sending. For where is he sent who is everywhere? The Spirit of the Lord, it says, has filled the whole world (Wisdom 1:7). And again: Lord, where shall I go from your Spirit, and where shall I flee from your face? If I ascend into heaven, you are there; and if I descend into hell, you are present. If I take my wings straight on, and dwell in the uttermost part of the sea: even there your hand will lead me, and your right hand will hold me (Psalm 138:7 ff.). Clearly no part of the world is left out where he did not show that the presence of the whole Trinity is. As we believe the Son sent according to the manhood, so [we believe] the Holy Spirit sent on account of the dove or the fire. But the Son so joined the assumed manhood to his person, for the sake of man, that he has it always, and never ceases [to have it], nor at any time receives an end; but the Holy Spirit [so joined] the dove or the fire that those visions, made in time, afterwards ceased to be.
CHAPTER VII.

There you have the reason why the Holy Spirit is said to be sent. But let these few things that we have said now be enough to strengthen your faith: that the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit are one God. He is certainly not a created nature, not earth, nor water, nor air, nor fire. For from these elements the bodies of living creatures are put together. He is certainly not an irrational spirit, as there is in cattle; nor a rational spirit, as there is in men or angels; but he is God, the unchangeable Trinity, creating all things through his goodness, created by no one. Who then can perceive even with the mind, as is fitting and as it truly is, that unwrought form by which all things were formed, much less express it in speech, except that God is thus believed and called Trinity? This uncreated Trinity, moreover, has implanted in its creation some traces, of whatever kind, of the Trinity. For so it is written, that he has ordered all things in number, in measure and in weight (Wisdom 11:21). Every body, that is, whether it be small or great, has both number according to the quantity of its parts, and has measure, and weight; nor could there be number without weight, or measure without weight and number. For wherever one of these is, it cannot be without the other two. But see, in bodily things weight, number and measure are easily demonstrated: let us see how they can be found in incorporeal things. In the soul of man, then, there are memory, counsel and will. For you think of what you will, which your memory also holds. For your will is your love. For you recall that which, by loving, you bring into your thought. They are three, memory, counsel, and will, which we have said is love, and they are inseparable, and they are one, and one cannot be without the other. One of the Fathers, too, elegantly said that these three are in the soul, when he prayed to God: "May I remember you, understand you, love you"; and he taught that the image of God is in these. For the human soul is the image of God, not begotten but created; not equal, but like.
CHAPTER VIII.

I have briefly set these things before your charity so that, since even in created things there are some signs of that supreme Trinity, it may be plain by evident reasoning how great is the error of the heretics, that, although in created things there is both trinity and unity, they do not believe that the very Trinity which is God is in unity of nature. By the power of this eternal and unchangeable Trinity all things were created; but we find that the more excellent and first to arise among creatures was the rational nature of angels, blessed by the gift of their God, and, through free will, not unceasingly clinging to [the One who] made it blessed. Of these a certain part of the angels, unwilling to do the will of its creator, was cast down from contemplating him and is kept to be punished at the judgement, as the apostle Peter says: God did not spare the angels who sinned, but, drawing them down with the chains of hell, delivered them into Tartarus to be kept for judgement, to be tormented (2 Peter 2:4). Deservedly indeed will they be punished for ever with the penalty of eternal fire: because, if they had wished to persevere in their blessedness, their free will would certainly have supported them. Through that will, turned to themselves, not to God, made dark through pride and thrust down into the lowest part of this air, they are kept to be punished at the judgement: no trace of good will has remained in them. But those who kept what they were made, through the same free will, that is, clinging unceasingly to God their creator, were made more blessed by the grace of God through their having stood firm: so much so that their will has neither the wish nor the power to sin; since, although they were made changeable by nature, they have been made unchangeable by grace: steadfast too, and certain that their blessedness will in no way be lost, they enjoy God, in the contemplation of whom they are blessed.
CHAPTER IX.

Great and learned men indeed assert that they are of a twofold substance, that is, of an incorporeal spirit, by which they never withdraw from the contemplation of God, and of a body, through which they appear to men from time to time, proving this from that place in the psalm where it says: Who makes his angels spirits, and his ministers a burning fire (Psalm 103:4). They say, then, that they have an ethereal body, that is, a fiery one; but the bad angels, that is, the demons, an airy body. So, after the fall of the bad and the steadfastness of the good, it pleased almighty God to found another rational creature, adorned with free will, by which that number of the angels falling from heaven which had perished might be filled up. I mean the first humans, put in their place, according to the soul from nothing, according to the body from clay: according to the soul, rational and immortal; but according to the body, immortal if he had not sinned; but if he sinned, mortal, that is, such that he could die, as the Apostle says, The body indeed is dead because of sin (Romans 8:10): since death was inflicted on the body as the penalty of sin. For besides the death of the spirit, in that it is forsaken by God, he received this also in the flesh: because, just as the life of the soul is to live blessedly, that is, to enjoy God, so to die is for the body to be forsaken by the soul. He would not have experienced the unequal penalty of these deaths, if he had not sinned. So man, made upright, and fashioned and formed to the image of his God in reason and understanding, received a law, by not transgressing which he would be blessed, since he had free will, so that he could be good if he wished, not indeed without the grace of God by which the will itself was governed so that it might will; and yet it was in his power to forsake that very grace when he wished. Because he willed it and sinned, for this he would also deservedly be condemned for eternity, and all his stock would be punished for ever with the transgressing angels, had not grace come upon them through Jesus Christ our Lord. For his death freed the human race from the power of the devil, to which it had been handed over to possess by a certain justice of God, and he ruled in them as in the sons of unbelief, as the Apostle says (Ephesians 5:6). So the death of Christ, which he underwent without sin, bestowed life on the sinner. The Only-begotten of God took up manhood, and the Word was made flesh, to perform the office of mediator between God and men: so that, since through free will we could by no means return to God, we might be able to return through God made man. Through this mediator, slain by the devil without cause, the devil himself, the author of death, lost those whom the same mediator judged by a hidden judgement.
CHAPTER X.

Let man not glory, then, in his merits, but let him who glories glory in the Lord (2 Corinthians 10:17). For what has he that he did not receive? And if he received it, why does he glory as if he had not received it (1 Corinthians 4:7)? For so the Lord himself says: If the Son sets you free, then you will be truly free (John 8:36). Our liberation lies in his decision, in his will. For wrath is in his anger, and life in his will (Psalm 29:6), says the Psalmist. Hence let the guilty man ascribe it to his own merits that he is condemned; that he is freed, to the grace of the Redeemer. Nor do we say this, that the human race has lost free will. For it has it, before it is freed by the grace of the Saviour, inclined to evil, not to good. Therefore free will itself is freed by the grace of God, so that it may will and be able [to do] good. For thus one of the Fathers (Augustine, Enchiridion ch. 32) says that the grace of God goes before the unwilling that he may will, and follows the willing, lest he will in vain. And so man, before he is a believer, has free will for evil; the believer has free will also for good, freed, that is, by the grace of God. Not undeservedly, then, do we obtain punishment for evil work, and eternal life for good.
CHAPTER XI.

Distinguishing, then, the grace which the first man had before sin from the grace by which men are now redeemed from the condemned mass of sin, someone says thus: The first is that man may have righteousness if he wishes; the second, then, is more powerful, by which it also comes about that he wishes, and wishes so much and loves with such ardour that by the will of the spirit he overcomes the pleasure of the flesh desiring contrary things. Nor indeed was that [first] small, by which even the power of free will was shown: since he was so helped that without this help he would not remain in good, but could forsake this help if he wished. This [second], however, is so much greater that it is too little for man to recover his lost liberty through it; too little, in short, not to be able without it either to lay hold of good or to remain in good if he wishes, unless it is also brought about that he wishes (Augustine, On Rebuke and Grace, ch. 11). What, then, comes first in this grace if not faith, which is to lead us to sight, so that we may see what we believe? Yet a man will not receive this faith unless he has been baptised in the name of the Trinity: so that, made a believer, he may know what to ask for and from whom, may seek and knock, so as to be able to find, as the Lord admonishes in the Gospel: Ask, and you will receive; seek, and you will find; knock, and it will be opened to you (Matthew 7:7). None are brought in but believers, unless they have been baptised in the name of the Trinity. Yet not all believers who are baptised will be saved: since indeed many heresies glory in this baptism of the Trinity, and seem to be baptised in the same way as the catholic Church; but they are held by great error, as long as they split the unity of the faith and refuse to communicate with the whole world, and for this reason they will deservedly be condemned. It profits them nothing, then, to be dipped in the name of the Trinity, who strive with rash presumption to divide the indivisible name of the Godhead itself. When indeed, pierced in heart, they return with humble piety to the catholic Church, the baptism which they have already received is not repeated in them, but they are reconciled through the laying on of the hand of the catholic Church. For thus that saying of the Lord is kept, Go, baptise all nations in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit (Matthew 28:19), that although they are baptised according to this rule outside the Church, or indeed within the Church by a bad and perverse priest, it is in no way repeated in them. For the faith which works through love is held by the holy catholic Church. This the heretics are shown in no way to have: because in truth faith alone is not enough, unless, believing in God, you love God and obey his commands. To obey his commands is not to do evil, and to do good, to fight against the devil, who strives at every moment to hinder our course as it tends towards God. Hence, according to the Apostle, like a roaring lion he goes about seeking whom he may devour (1 Peter 5:8): he must be resisted strongly in faith.
CHAPTER XII.

And although, as long as we live mortally in this world, we cannot be without sin, yet [we must take care] that we are not entangled in any crimes, so that we may return to his service, and, having been made his vessels, he may begin again to dwell in us. What criminal sins are, both divine Scripture and the laws of the world punish publicly; and your conscience too is not ignorant of what it does not wish to suffer from another. But if perhaps after baptism we have become entangled in some crimes, let us not be reluctant to do penance, and with contrite heart and body to ask forgiveness from God. For those who think they commit sins with impunity, while perhaps they give some alms to the poor, are much deceived. For they do not know that the first work of mercy is to offer oneself to God, and so to show mercy to another. For thus Scripture says: Have mercy on your own soul, pleasing God (Ecclesiasticus 30:24); and again: He who is wicked to himself, to whom will he be good? (Ecclesiasticus 14:5). Therefore alms must be given, but vices must first be abandoned. They differ much, then, from those who have kept their garment white, who, with the Lord's help, persevere to the end of their departure such as they were when reborn: for them daily prayer suffices to loose the least faults which creep in in this mortal body; from which the Apostle longs to be freed, saying: Unhappy man that I am! Who will free me from the body of this death? The grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord (Romans 7:24). For the Lord too in the Gospel (Matthew 13:23) showed three fruitfulnesses of the earth, that is, he showed three grades of the good in the Church: thirtyfold, sixtyfold and hundredfold. Hence also Noah's ark, which signified the Church, was of two storeys and three storeys, signifying, as we have said, three grades or orders, which the expositors of the Church have referred to the married, the continent and virgins: the thirtyfold, namely, to the married, the sixtyfold to the continent, the hundredfold to virgins. So too the catholic Church is established in these grades, so that, although there are three grades, there are nevertheless many differences of merits. For neither do all virgins receive the reward of the kingdom of heaven equally, nor all the continent, nor all the married: but each will receive his own wage, says the Apostle, according to his own labour (1 Corinthians 3:8). And the more one has been obedient to God than another, the more wage he will receive. And what will that wage or reward be, unless God himself will be the reward of virtue? Someone has said: He who gave virtue, who gave victory to those who strive, will himself without doubt be the crown. By which we understand that one will see God in that life the more than another, the more he loved him in this life and was obedient to his commands.
CHAPTER XIII.

But in the very flesh of the dead who rise again there will also be many differences of glory, as the Apostle says: One is the glory of the sun, another the glory of the moon, another the glory of the stars. For star differs from star in glory; so also will be the resurrection of the dead (1 Corinthians 15:41). Therefore whatever bodies either fire has consumed, or a beast devoured, or water swallowed up, will rise in that moment of time and in the twinkling of an eye, each in the sex in which he died: the male, then, in the male, and the female in the female. That the dead rise, the Lord says in the Gospel: Have you not read what the Lord says to Moses from the bush: I am the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob (Luke 20:37)? And continuing he adds: He is not the God of the dead, but of the living. For all live to him (ibid., 38); and again: Then, he says, all who are in the tombs will hear the voice of the Son of God, and those who have done good will rise to the resurrection of life, but those who have done evil to the resurrection of judgement (John 5:28, 29). For elsewhere too (Matthew 25:46), enumerating the works of mercy and rebuking the good and the wicked, he says that these will go into eternal punishment. The good, moreover, everlasting joy will receive, where they will reign with their God without end, and, secure in their own stability, nothing unseemly will delight them. For wherever their spirit will be, [it will be] at once in the new heaven and the new earth. But the wicked eternal fire will receive, which will torment them for ever, where their worm will not die and the fire will not be quenched (Mark 9:44). Therefore, dearest one, we must strive, and continually implore the mercy of God, that we may live soberly, piously and justly in this world, so that we may be able to come to the kingdom of heaven.
